First steps — why uniqueness needs an assumption

This example deliberately starts with a counterexample: existence does not imply uniqueness. In Use this history; find facts mode, the checker chooses truth values for chosen(red) and chosen(blue). SomeChoice requires at least one, but permits both; UniqueChoice requires exactly one. A model with both values chosen therefore satisfies the assumption and falsifies the property. No protocol events or intermediate time stages are needed: even the empty history has its end-of-time world.

To supply the missing guarantee, choose Edit Markdown, change the formula of SomeChoice to ∃¹ v. chosen(v), choose Update choices, and run again. With the starting selections, UniqueChoice then holds within the selected scope. A supplied-model check has a different task: it evaluates the explicit facts, treating absent facts as false.

Use Return to previous example and Continue to next example to browse the curated set. Loading another example clears the preceding results; it does not run the new example automatically.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Assumptions and protocol rules

SomeChoice — other assumption

At least one domain value is chosen. Both values may still be chosen.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Definition 3.3.3, p. 20.
axiom SomeChoice [other]:
  ∃ v. chosen(v)

Properties to check

These claims test the declared finite scenario. Their validity scope is shown on each property.

UniqueChoice — property

Exactly one domain value is chosen. The existential assumption above does not supply uniqueness.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Definition 3.6.1, p. 26; Figure 5, p. 27.
property UniqueChoice [end]:
  ∃¹ v. chosen(v)

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Paper draft: Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, 2026-11-07. References use the draft's printed page numbers.

Sections 2-4 supply the semantics, not these example claims: history structures (Definition 2.3.5, p. 11), syntax/signatures (Definitions 3.1.1 and 3.1.3, pp. 17-18), models and interpreted predicates (Definition 3.3.3, p. 20), validity (Definition 3.4.10 and Figure 3, pp. 24-25), and uniqueness sugar (Definition 3.6.1 and Figure 5, pp. 26-27).

Pedagogical logic scenario, not a literal paper theory: chosen, SomeChoice, and UniqueChoice are introduced only here. No HBB axioms or correctness theorem are asserted. The proposed edit strengthens ∃ to ∃¹ to supply the uniqueness that ordinary existence lacks.

ThyHBB1 — completed broadcast

This is a completed one-participant run of ThyHBB1, using the axioms and correctness statements from the draft of 7 November 2026. Choose Use this history; find facts first. The given positive facts pin liveness and safety; the retained axioms constrain the remaining predicate interpretation.

The final silent † tuple records knowledge of delivery. It is not an extra protocol event. Removing that observation can violate the Knowledge scheme, even though delivery itself has occurred.

The correctness formulas include their stated premises. A true implication may be vacuous. For a direct non-vacuity investigation, the API supplies the corresponding scenario formulas through correctnessProperties("ThyHBB1"). In this completed singleton example all three scenarios occur.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⁰¹ v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If safety holds at every actual local tuple, a live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.5.3, p. 48.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.4.5, p. 47.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Paper and interpretation

Implementation authorship: this executable theory was AI-generated following prompts by Murdoch J. Gabbay. Automated validation is described in the package; no independent expert audit of this translation is claimed. Source-paper authorship is listed separately.

Paper draft: Heterogeneous trust in reliable broadcast via modal logic and history structures, Murdoch J. Gabbay and Isaac Sheff, 2026-11-07. References use the draft's printed page numbers.

Paper basis: ThyHBB1, Definition 6.1.2, pp. 41-42; Figure 7, p. 41. Correctness: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43. Proofs: Liveness 1: Proposition 6.5.3, p. 48; Liveness 2: Proposition 6.4.5, p. 47; Agreement: Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.

Pedagogical completed-run scenario: the protocol axioms and conditional correctness formulas in this document are unmodified translations of the paper. The singleton history, positive facts and final observation are supplied for this example; they are not a literal paper theory or a proof over all histories.

Code event order: propose(v), echo(v), vote(l,v), and deliver(m,l,v): m is the reporting learner, l the source learner, and v the value (Notation 6.1.3 and Remark 6.1.4, p. 42). HBB3 instead uses the pair deliver(l,v). Learners and values share one domain (Definition 3.1.1, p. 17).

include ThyLive keeps Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4 dynamic: LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both complete Knowledge schemes, over all ground events and all finite learner lists (including empty lists and repetitions), are checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37). The schemes regenerate when the history changes. Full source and notation map; paper variants and their status.

HBB1: remove Echo!

A live participant knows the unique proposal and never echoes. The curated browser preset omits Echo!, admitting a model in which Liveness 1 fails with its complete premise and trigger true. Liveness 2 and Agreement hold vacuously because there are no deliveries. Restoring Echo! makes the full theory incompatible with this fixed history, so all three claims are then Not tested. Both runs use exactly the same history and facts. Final silent observations preserve the complete Knowledge schemes.

Browser preset: only Echo! is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "Echo!".

HBB1: remove Vote!

A live participant knows the unique proposal, echoes it, and never votes. Safety is pinned true at all times, exercising the distinctive persistent-safety premise of HBB1 Vote!. The curated browser preset omits Vote!, admitting a model in which Liveness 1 fails with its complete premise and trigger true. Liveness 2 and Agreement have absent scenarios. Restoring Vote! makes the full theory incompatible with this fixed history, leaving the claims Not tested. Final silent observations preserve the complete Knowledge schemes.

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2; Remark 6.2.2, p. 44.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⁰¹ v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If safety holds at every actual local tuple, a live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.5.3, p. 48.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.4.5, p. 47.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

HBB1: remove Deliver!

Both live participants echo and vote; p delivers, while q observes delivery and never delivers. Safety is pinned true everywhere, including the exact global safety premise of Liveness 2. The curated browser preset omits Deliver!, admitting a model in which Liveness 1 and Liveness 2 fail at q with their complete premises and triggers true. Agreement holds with its scenario present. Restoring Deliver! makes the full theory incompatible with this fixed history, leaving the claims Not tested. Final silent observations preserve the complete Knowledge schemes.

HBB1: remove the Safe definition

A live singleton proposes and echoes the unique value, then stops before voting. Safety has no supplied positive facts. In the given interpretation safe(v) is false, so only Safe fails: Vote! is disabled by its persistent-safety premise. With Safe retained, its at-most-one-proposal disjunct forces safe(v) everywhere, enabling Vote! and making this stopped history inconsistent. Omitting only Safe permits safe(v) to remain false and gives a nonvacuous Liveness 1 counterexample. The other two correctness scenarios are absent.

This is a genuine HBB1 definition-removal experiment, not one of the paper's stated incorrect-axiom variants. It uses Remark 6.2.2, p. 44, and Lemma 6.5.2, pp. 47–48: at most one proposed value implies safety. The paired full and omitted rows change only the retained rule selection; the correctness property itself is unchanged.

HBB1: a live participant chooses one echo value

The live sequential singleton observes proposals a and b, chooses only echo(a), votes a for both learners and completes all reporting/source deliveries of a. The correct existential Echo! accepts this model; all three complete correctness conditionals hold. Liveness 1 has an absent scenario because its unique-proposal premise is false. Liveness 2 and Agreement have present scenarios. Sequential quorum intersections make Safe true even with multiple proposals.

The extra Bad Echo! property is a diagnostic probe of the universally closed incorrect axiom in Remark 6.2.3(2), p. 44: (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ↕ echo(w) for all v,w. It fails at a live world with known proposal a and w=b because echo(b) never occurs. It is not a failed correctness theorem. The paired incorrect-axiom example replaces only Echo! with that formula and has no model. Requiring all values to be echoed overconstrains the choice and conflicts here with EchoNE.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2; Remark 6.2.2, p. 44.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⁰¹ v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If safety holds at every actual local tuple, a live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.5.3, p. 48.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.4.5, p. 47.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Bad Echo! — diagnostic probe

This diagnostic tests the explicitly incorrect universally closed Echo! from Remark 6.2.3(2), p. 44. A failure refutes that candidate axiom, rather than a correctness theorem.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim. Remark 6.2.3(2), p. 44.
property Bad Echo! [all]:
  ∀ v,w. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ↕ echo(w)

HBB1: the incorrect universal Echo! overconstrains choice

This example has exactly the history, facts, quorums and correctness properties of the valid one-echo choice model. It changes only Echo!, replacing its existentially chosen conclusion by the incorrect formula printed in Remark 6.2.3(2), p. 44, with both free variables universally closed.

The live participant knows proposals a and b but echoes only a. The bad axiom demands eventual echo(b) as well; this fixed history has no model. All three correctness claims are Not tested after that consistency failure. This is an overconstraint demonstration, not a correctness counterexample. In an extension that echoes both distinct values at the singleton, EchoNE would also forbid that choice. The valid example separately probes this precise bad formula and supplies a replayable counterexample to the probe.

HBB1: full Vote? rejects unsafe votes

Source learners a and b have disjoint singleton quorums {q} and {r}; reporting learner c has the sequential singleton quorum {p}. Participant q echoes a and r echoes b without local equivocation. Participant p votes for the two different source learners and delivers both values via reporter c. The exact Safe definition is retained; positive facts record its true instances at the declared prefixes. After both proposals, the disjoint intersections make these learners unsafe. A scenario-only NoLive axiom keeps all participants non-live, so the forward obligations are vacuous. The example therefore isolates safety from liveness.

This full-guard control has no model: the correct Vote? requires safe(l), which is false at the offending votes. All three correctness claims are therefore Not tested.

The omitted-guard companion deletes only that conjunct, leaving quorum support, EchoNE, Safe and all ThyLive schemes intact. That edited theory admits a nonvacuous Agreement counterexample on the same history. In that counterexample, both reporting variables of Agreement are assigned learner c, its source variables l and m are assigned learners a and b, and the delivered values are the distinct a and b. HBB1 Agreement constrains reporting intersections; the distinct source quorums need not intersect. Both liveness scenarios are absent. This deliberate local weakening is not claimed to be one of the paper's incorrect examples; its relevance follows from Figure 7 and the Agreement proof, Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.

axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires both current safe(l) and knowledge of a quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ (safe(l) ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Safe — other assumption

Safety is a biconditional: at most one proposal value is known, or every learner has a sequential witness in every relevant quorum intersection.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2; Remark 6.2.2, p. 44.
axiom Safe [other]:
  ∀ l. safe(l) ⇔ ((∃⁰¹ v. ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ∨ (∀ m. ♢[l,m] seq))

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

If safety holds at every actual local tuple, a live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. ⇕ safe(l) ⇒ (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 7, p. 41; Definition 6.1.2.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.5.3, p. 48.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant. The source learner must also be safe at every participant at the end of time.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.4.5, p. 47.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live) ∧ (□[] safe(l))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒
  ↕ deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 8, p. 41; Theorem 6.1.6, p. 43; Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[a,b] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

HBB1: omit only the safety guard from Vote?

Source learners a and b have disjoint singleton quorums {q} and {r}; reporting learner c has the sequential singleton quorum {p}. Participant q echoes a and r echoes b without local equivocation. Participant p votes for the two different source learners and delivers both values via reporter c. The exact Safe definition is retained; positive facts record its true instances at the declared prefixes. After both proposals, the disjoint intersections make these learners unsafe. A scenario-only NoLive axiom keeps all participants non-live, so the forward obligations are vacuous. The example therefore isolates safety from liveness.

This edited theory has an Agreement counterexample: it deletes only the safe(l) conjunct from Vote?, leaving quorum support, EchoNE, Safe and all ThyLive schemes intact. The full-guard control on the same history has no model because that conjunct is false at the offending votes.

In that counterexample, both reporting variables of Agreement are assigned learner c, its source variables l and m are assigned learners a and b, and the delivered values are the distinct a and b. HBB1 Agreement constrains reporting intersections; the distinct source quorums need not intersect. Both liveness scenarios are absent. This deliberate local weakening is not claimed to be one of the paper's incorrect examples; its relevance follows from Figure 7 and the Agreement proof, Proposition 6.3.1, p. 45.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

ThyHBB2 — completed broadcast

This is a completed one-participant run of ThyHBB2, using the axioms and correctness statements from the draft of 7 November 2026. Choose Use this history; find facts first. The given positive facts pin liveness; the retained axioms constrain the remaining predicate interpretation.

The final silent † tuple records knowledge of delivery. It is not an extra protocol event. Removing that observation can violate the Knowledge scheme, even though delivery itself has occurred.

The correctness formulas include their stated premises. A true implication may be vacuous. For a direct non-vacuity investigation, the API supplies the corresponding scenario formulas through correctnessProperties("ThyHBB2"). In this completed singleton example all three scenarios occur.

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires knowledge of a source quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ echo(v)

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.3, p. 53.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.2, p. 52.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

What EchoNE rules out

This deliberately unsuitable history is a single sequential chain: red and blue are proposed, both are echoed, and both are voted for and delivered. NoLive makes the participant non-live; it remains sequential.

The curated browser preset omits EchoNE. Run Use this history; find facts to find a model in which Agreement is false: its sequential quorum-intersection premise holds, but the two delivered values differ.

Choose Keep all axioms for the comparison. EchoNE then rejects the real conflicting echoes, and changing predicate truth values cannot repair this fixed history. The result is no model, with all correctness claims Not tested; it is not an Agreement proof. In the omission run, both liveness claims hold with absent scenarios: NoLive excludes their live-quorum premise, and two distinct values are proposed. The saved evidence records the omission and can be replayed. All three full correctness formulas are checked by node demo.mjs.

Browser preset: only EchoNE is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "EchoNE".

When EchoNE constrains only live participants

This uses exactly the sequential two-value history and NoLive assumption from echo-ne.md. Every declared axiom is retained, including the complete dynamic ThyLive include. The only edit to the protocol is EchoNE: its prohibition now applies only when the participant is live.

Use this history; find facts finds a model of all the edited assumptions, yet Agreement fails with a sequential quorum intersection and two conflicting deliveries. NoLive makes the weakened EchoNE true without excluding those echoes; ThyLive permits a non-live participant to be sequential. Liveness 1 and Liveness 2 hold with absent scenarios.

The unedited EchoNE on this same history gives no model, which is not a proof of Agreement. This concrete countermodel shows that the live-only restriction loses this Agreement guarantee for the selected finite scope. It makes no unbounded claim about all weakenings. Run node demo.mjs for the full comparison and independently replayed evidence.

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.2, p. 52.
property Liveness 2 [end]:

  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires knowledge of a source quorum of prior matching echoes.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ echo(v)

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a reporting quorum of matching source-learner votes.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.3, p. 53.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.2, p. 52.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

  ∀ m,l,v. deliver(m,l,v) ⇒ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for that value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ↕ vote(l,v)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with a reporting quorum of votes must deliver the indicated reporting learner, source learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 9, p. 50; Definition 7.1.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ m,l,v. (live ∧ □[m] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(m,l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.3, p. 53.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.2, p. 52.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,v. ((♢[a,b] ⊤) ∧ (□[b] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(b,l,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 10, p. 50; Theorem 7.1.3, p. 51; Proposition 7.3.1, p. 52.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ a,b,l,m,v,w. ((♢[l,m] seq)) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(a,l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(b,m,w)) ⇒
  v=w)

ThyHBB3 — completed broadcast

This is a completed one-participant run of ThyHBB3, using the axioms and correctness statements from the draft of 7 November 2026. Choose Use this history; find facts first. The given positive facts pin liveness and correlation; the retained axioms constrain the remaining predicate interpretation.

The final silent † tuple records knowledge of delivery. It is not an extra protocol event. Removing that observation can violate the Knowledge scheme, even though delivery itself has occurred.

The correctness formulas include their stated premises. A true implication may be vacuous. For a direct non-vacuity investigation, the API supplies the corresponding scenario formulas through correctnessProperties("ThyHBB3"). In this completed singleton example all three scenarios occur.

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for some value for that learner somewhere in its actual local run. The chosen value remains existential.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

With correlation at every actual local tuple and knowledge of a correlated learner’s vote, a live participant must vote for some value for the target learner somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum votes must deliver that learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59-60.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.4.5, p. 59.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Paper and interpretation

The paper writes correlation as l ≐ m. In Figure 11, p. 56, CorrSeq, CorrPast, CorrSymm and CorrTran denote ≐seq, ≐⇓, ≐symm and ≐tran. The executable predicate is corr(l,m). Correlation is distinct from value equality; both voting forward rules retain the paper’s existential value choice.

A live proposal stops before echoing

This is a pedagogical Echo! omission. The complete protocol chain would be proposal → echo → vote → delivery. This supplied history has one live sequential participant and stops after the proposal. The final silent † tuple observes the latest real event and supplies the eventual knowledge required by ThyLive; it is not an additional protocol action.

Echo! is the sole failed original rule. Removing it leaves a known unique proposal but no echo, vote, or delivery, so Liveness 1 fails with its premise and trigger true. Liveness 2 and Agreement have absent scenarios. The progress rules are Figure 11; compare Liveness 1’s proof in Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59–60.

Browser preset: only Echo! is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "Echo!".

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59–60.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.4.5, p. 59.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

A live echo stops before voting

This is a pedagogical Vote! omission. The complete protocol chain would be proposal → echo → vote → delivery. This supplied history has one live sequential participant and stops after the echo. The final silent † tuple observes the latest real event and supplies the eventual knowledge required by ThyLive; it is not an additional protocol action.

Vote! is the sole failed original rule. Removing it leaves a quorum echo of the known unique value but no vote or delivery, so Liveness 1 fails nonvacuously. Vote'! remains selected: it has no source vote from which to propagate, so it does not repair this prefix. Liveness 2 and Agreement have absent scenarios. The progress rules are Figure 11; compare Liveness 1’s proof in Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59–60.

Browser preset: only Vote! is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "Vote!".

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for some value for that learner somewhere in its actual local run. The chosen value remains existential.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

With correlation at every actual local tuple and knowledge of a correlated learner’s vote, a live participant must vote for some value for the target learner somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum votes must deliver that learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59–60.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Correlation propagation without Vote'!

This is a pedagogical Vote'! omission, specifically exercising Liveness 2. The two live participants propose different values and each echoes only its own value. Learner a has quorum {p}; learner b has quorum {p,q}. Both participants vote for and deliver a’s value, with final silent observations ensuring the complete Knowledge schemes hold. Every learner is correlated everywhere, and all local histories are sequential. The mixed echo quorum {p,q} never unanimously supports any value, so Vote! cannot initiate a b-vote.

The source a-vote activates Vote'!, which is the sole failed original rule. Omitting it prevents any b-delivery, so Liveness 2 fails with correlation, a live b-quorum, and source delivery all present. Liveness 1’s unique-proposal scenario is absent; Agreement holds with a delivery scenario present. The rule’s role is discussed in Proposition 8.4.5, p. 59, and footnote 54, p. 57: the paper’s ⇕ corr premise is deliberate.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for some value for that learner somewhere in its actual local run. The chosen value remains existential.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

With correlation at every actual local tuple and knowledge of a correlated learner’s vote, a live participant must vote for some value for the target learner somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum votes must deliver that learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59–60.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.4.5, p. 59.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

A correlated fork without CorrSeq

This is a pedagogical CorrSeq omission, not the literal full theory. One participant has two incomparable causal branches, each with its own proposal, echo, vote, and delivery. Both values use the singleton quorum. Each branch satisfies the backward rules; because neither branch contains the other, EchoNE and VoteNE see no earlier conflicting event. Correlation is pinned everywhere. At the end that participant is not sequential, so CorrSeq alone rejects the history. Omitting CorrSeq admits both different deliveries: Agreement fails with its correlation premise and delivery trigger present. Both liveness scenarios are absent. The paper explains the role of sequential quorum intersections in Agreement’s proof, Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.

  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)

Correlation learned too late without CorrPast

This is a pedagogical CorrPast omission. The participant r forks, while s is sequential. A first vote for learner c supports votes for a through a local correlation class {a,c}; a separate echo branch supports b. Learners a and b each have quorum {r,s}, and c has quorum {r}. The sequential member s witnesses CorrSeq for a and b at the end. Only at the end does the supplied interpretation relate a to b at every participant. Because that relation was absent at the sequential conflicting votes, VoteNE does not apply there.

CorrPast is the sole failed original rule; omitting it makes Agreement false with its complete end-of-time premise and both deliveries present. Both liveness scenarios are absent. See the backward persistence used in Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57, and the valid alternate temporal formulation in Remark 8.3.2, p. 57.

The added NoLive scenario rule fixes live false. Consequently the forward rules and both Knowledge schemes remain present and hold; these examples exercise safety, not progress. This is an explicit model scenario, not a proposed replacement for a paper axiom.

Browser preset: only CorrPast is omitted. Keep all axioms selects the full-theory comparison; Use example defaults restores the omission. Neither action starts a run. The source declares every rule: plain Markdown imports and CLI runs retain them unless you specify --drop "CorrPast".

Read the rules below, choose Continue to claims, review the selected properties and assumptions, then continue to the run settings and run the check. Use Edit Markdown to change a rule; Unicode and ASCII spellings have identical semantics. The supplied history JSON is at the end.

Shared liveness assumptions

The complete dynamic ThyLive theory includes LiveAlways, LiveSeq, and both Knowledge schemes. The schemes are generated for the current history; every included assumption is checked at all possible worlds.

# Paper: Figure 6, p. 38, Definition 5.2.4; full dynamic LiveAlways, LiveSeq and both Knowledge schemes, checked at all possible worlds (Definition 5.2.1, p. 37).
include ThyLive

Assumptions and protocol rules

NoLive — other assumption

This scenario assumption makes every participant non-live at every possible world. It isolates the safety question from liveness obligations.

# Scenario: added for this experiment; not a paper axiom or correctness claim.
axiom NoLive [other]:
  ¬ live

Echo? — backward rule

An echo must be justified by knowledge of a proposal of that value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Echo? [backward]:
  ∀ v. echo(v) ⇒ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)

Vote? — backward rule

A vote requires either quorum echoes of that value, or knowledge of a matching vote for a currently correlated learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. vote(l,v) ⇒ ((□[l] ↓ echo(v)) ∨ (∃ m. (corr(m,l) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v))))

Deliver? — backward rule

Delivery requires knowledge of a quorum of matching votes for the same learner.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Deliver? [backward]:
  ∀ l,v. deliver(l,v) ⇒ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)

EchoNE — other assumption

A participant cannot echo a value different from one at an earlier actual local echo. Incomparable forks are not ordered by this rule.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom EchoNE [other]:
  ∀ v,w. echo(v) ⇒ ↓ echo(w) ⇒ v=w

VoteNE — other assumption

An actual local vote and an earlier local vote for correlated learners must carry the same value.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom VoteNE [other]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. vote(l,v) ⇒ ↓ vote(m,w) ⇒ corr(l,m) ⇒ v=w

3twined — other assumption

Every triple of independently chosen learner quorums must have a common participant. Repeated learner names still make independent quorum choices.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom 3twined [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. ♢[l,m,n] ⊤

CorrSeq — other assumption

For every choice of one quorum from each correlated learner, their intersection must contain a sequential participant.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrSeq [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ♢[l,m] seq

CorrPast — other assumption

Correlation persists to every actual earlier local tuple. Its temporal operator ranges over recorded local tuples, rather than every hypothetical world.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrPast [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ ⇓ corr(l,m)

CorrSymm — other assumption

Correlation is symmetric. Reflexivity is not an additional assumption.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrSymm [other]:
  ∀ l,m. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,l)

CorrTran — other assumption

Correlation is transitive.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom CorrTran [other]:
  ∀ l,m,n. corr(l,m) ⇒ corr(m,n) ⇒ corr(l,n)

Echo! — forward rule

A live participant that knows a proposal must echo some value somewhere in its actual local run. The value is existentially chosen.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Echo! [forward]:
  ∀ v. (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ echo(w)

Vote! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum echoes must vote for some value for that learner somewhere in its actual local run. The chosen value remains existential.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ echo(v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Vote'! — forward rule

With correlation at every actual local tuple and knowledge of a correlated learner’s vote, a live participant must vote for some value for the target learner somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Vote'! [forward]:
  ∀ l,m,v. (live ∧ ⇕ corr(l,m) ∧ ♢[] ↓ vote(m,v)) ⇒ ∃ w. ↕ vote(l,w)

Deliver! — forward rule

A live participant with quorum votes must deliver that learner and value somewhere in its actual local run.

# Paper: Figure 11, p. 56; Definition 8.2.1, p. 55.
axiom Deliver! [forward]:
  ∀ l,v. (live ∧ □[l] ↓ vote(l,v)) ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v)

Properties to check

Each correctness claim keeps its complete conditional premises. If its premises and trigger never occur together, the claim can hold vacuously. The experiment report records whether that full scenario occurs.

Liveness 1 — correctness claim

Under the displayed live-quorum and unique-proposal premises, the proposal-knowledge trigger requires delivery at each live participant. All premises and triggers are part of the checked formula.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.5.1, pp. 59–60.
property Liveness 1 [end]:
  ∀ l,v. ((□[l] live) ∧ (∃¹ w. ♢[] ↓ propose(w))) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ (live ∧ ♢[] ↓ propose(v)) ⇒
  live ⇒ ↕ deliver(l,v))

Liveness 2 — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust and liveness premises, known delivery for the source learner requires delivery for the target learner at each live participant.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.4.5, p. 59.
property Liveness 2 [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v. ((□[] corr(l,m)) ∧ (□[m] live)) ⇒ (♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v) ⇒ live ⇒ ↕
  deliver(m,v))

Agreement — correctness claim

Under the displayed trust premise, the two known deliveries must have the same broadcast value.

# Paper: Figure 12, p. 56; Theorem 8.2.3, p. 57; Proposition 8.3.1, p. 57.
property Agreement [end]:
  ∀ l,m,v,w. ((□[] corr(l,m))) ⇒ ((♢[] ↓ deliver(l,v)) ∧ (♢[] ↓ deliver(m,w)) ⇒ v=w)
